category_summaries.summary: The Employer recognizes UFCW Local No. 408 as the exclusive collective bargaining agent for all Meat Department employees in the Employer’s retail stores located in specified Texas counties, and the contract’s jurisdiction covers Meat Department work in those counties regardless of where performed (so long as such work continues to be performed by the Employer, is within the covered geographical area, and is not already represented by another union). The Employer must also continue to recognize the Union’s jurisdiction over existing delicatessen operations in its stores. The agreement binds the Employer’s successors/assigns, and if ownership changes, the Company must pay employees accumulated wage obligations and pro rata earned vacation or other monetary benefits under the agreement at the time of transfer. During the contract term, the Employer must weekly deduct initiation fees and regular union dues from union members who voluntarily authorize such deductions in writing, and remit the deducted amounts to Local Union No. 408 monthly; separately, where no employee credit union exists, the Employer must make weekly credit union deductions for employees who request them and remit to the UFCW Local No. 408 Federal Credit Union. The Employer must recognize the Union’s right to designate one Shop Steward per market (in writing), and union shop cards may be displayed in markets employing union members, with removal authorized by the Local Union Secretary-Treasurer or agent for contract violations. The Union also classifies newly employed employees regarding qualification for Journeymen and Apprentices.

The agreement provides that each shop must have a Head Meat Cutter who is a Journeyman Meat Cutter, responsible for directing the work, movements, and operations of Meat Department employees and performing all related duties. Management and direction of store operations—including planning, directing, expanding or reducing operations, controlling and operating the workplace, hiring, assigning, suspending or discharging for proper cause, relieving employees due to lack of work or other proper reasons, introducing new or improved methods or facilities, and establishing necessary rules and regulations—are vested exclusively in the Employer. The Employer also retains all rights it had before the Agreement, except where expressly limited, and must furnish any promulgated rules and regulations to the Union and either post them on bulletin boards or provide copies to employees. Additionally, late/night shift work cannot be assigned for disciplinary reasons, and the Employer may release an employee for any cause without recourse if the release occurs within thirty (30) days of the employee’s employment.

The Employer will credit full-time employees for comparable retail food industry experience that was formally specified on the employment application and was within the three (3) years immediately prior to hire (excluding military service). Proof must be furnished by the employee or determined by the Employer within thirty (30) days after hire; any resulting pay increase takes effect as of the verification date. Journeyman Meat Cutters assigned to relieve the Head Meat Cutter for more than two (2) consecutive scheduled working days receive the Head Meat Cutter rate for hours actually worked, excluding the Head Meat Cutter’s regular scheduled days off from the calculation. Overtime applies to hours over forty (40) in a workweek at time-and-one-half (1½); additional overtime rules apply when a holiday falls—hours over thirty-two (32) (or twenty-four (24) if two holidays fall in the same workweek) are paid at 1½. Sunday work is paid at not less than 1½, and holiday work is paid at not less than two (2) times the regular rate for hours worked. Time spent traveling during the workday between two stores at the Employer’s request is counted as time worked, and eligible employees using their own transportation receive fifteen cents (15c) per mile. Part-time employees scheduled to work a recognized holiday but who fail to report or do not work the scheduled hours (including the scheduled day before or after) are not eligible for holiday pay. Wage progression increases under Appendix A continue during the Agreement’s life with no change to progression rates, but service does not accrue during wage-determination leave of absence periods exceeding thirty (30) days; upon return, accrual resumes. If a store is closed or sold and employees are terminated, employees receive pro rata vacation and severance pay of one (1) week’s pay per year of continuous service commencing with the third (3rd) year, capped at not more than eight (8) weeks at their regular rate, with pro rata severance for incomplete years. Severance is computed using average hours worked over the fifty-two (52) weeks preceding a voluntary layoff/termination, and all monies due (including severance) are paid in a lump sum upon termination. Certain employees in specified progression classifications receive progression increases during the Agreement; for other specified classifications (Head Meat Cutter, Journeyman Meat Cutter, and Weighers and Wrappers “Thereafter” only), increases are pro rata based on average hours worked in the preceding twelve (12) months, and a specific pro rata lump-sum calculation applies to eligible employees on approved leave of absence and/or layoff as of November 18, 1984. Employees receiving above-minimum hourly rates are not reduced except as provided for the Seafood Department, and “red circled” Seafood Clerks electing to remain in the Seafood Department remain at their current rate until they would otherwise receive an increase within the Seafood rate scale.

Full-time work is scheduled by the Employer and consists of a 40-hour workweek worked in five days; employees scheduled for 40 hours in a week are guaranteed 40 hours (or pay in lieu) for that week except on days the employee is tardy, absent, or disciplined for just cause, and the guarantee does not apply when time off is granted by mutual agreement or for defined emergencies. Employees receive two 15-minute paid rest periods each day (before and after lunch), lunch periods not exceeding one hour, and an additional 15-minute rest period after the 10th hour worked if required to work more than 10 hours in a day. Any time over 8 hours in a day and any work after the 5th full day in a workweek is overtime at a minimum rate of 1½ times the regular basic rate; there are no split shifts. Schedules are posted for full-time employees by 4:00 p.m. Friday for the succeeding week (including Sunday/holiday) and cannot be changed during the week without employee consent except for sickness or emergencies (e.g., strike, fire, flood); schedules also may not be changed to avoid overtime except as allowed. Employees required to work on a scheduled day off receive 1½ times pay for that day. An employee reporting as scheduled without prior notice not to report is guaranteed the scheduled day’s minimum hours or 4 hours/pay, whichever is greater, absent emergencies. No employee may be required to work more than five hours without an unpaid lunch. Time spent attending Company-sponsored meetings outside scheduled work hours is treated as time worked, and employees must not be required to report for work until they have had at least 10 hours off duty. Part-time schedules are posted by 4:00 p.m. Friday, may be changed during the week due to business conditions, and are based on seniority within classification up to 8 hours in a day/40 hours in a week, subject to qualification/availability and without creating additional contract premiums/penalties; part-time employees must notify the Store Manager within 24 hours after posting to claim posted hours, and the most senior qualified immediately available employees receive the most hours. During the Agreement term, the Employer will not reduce scheduled hours of regular full-time employees on the payroll as of November 15, 1980, except as allowed under a side letter. A full-time employee may opt to work less than 40 hours but not less than 32 hours per week at their store, which waives the right to file a time claim.

Part-time employees become eligible for paid vacation only after completing twelve (12) months of continuous service and working at least six hundred twenty-four (624) straight-time hours during the applicable twelve-month anniversary year, entitling them on their anniversary date to one (1) week of pro-rated paid vacation calculated as total hours worked in that anniversary year divided by fifty-two (52) weeks. After three (3) years’ service, part-timers receive a second (2nd) pro-rated vacation week, with two (2) weeks being the maximum allowable for part-timers. If an employee is reduced from full-time to part-time due to a reduction in employer work hours, previously earned vacation (if any) is retained and pro-rated by dividing total hours worked in the vacation qualifying year by 52. Full-time vacation eligibility is based on continuous full-time service anniversaries: one (1) week after the first anniversary; additional eligibility rules provide for a one-week vacation as of January 1 for those with one (1) year service prior to January 1, a second week after three (3) years (including an as-of-January-1 two-week rule for those with three (3) years prior to January 1), further increases to three (3) weeks after seven (7) years, four (4) weeks after fifteen (15) years, and five (5) weeks after twenty (20) years; employees may take earned 1–4 week vacations early or wait until later in the year if they later complete service for an additional week. Vacation is computed from the date of employment/anniversary date and is taken at a mutually convenient time; it is paid at the employee’s current weekly rate, with the employer consulting the Head Meat Cutter and a Union representative on whether replacements are needed, and the employer’s decision being conclusive if there is disagreement after due consideration. When a holiday occurs during the calendar week of vacation, the employee may elect an extra day of vacation or pay in lieu. Vacation pay is paid prior to the vacation period; employees are not given pay in lieu of vacation unless mutually agreed by the employer, employee, and Union. If a full-time employee is terminated before taking earned vacation (except for dishonesty), vacation pay is paid at termination. Leave of absence affects vacation earned after one (1) year of employment: leaves totaling 90 days or less in a calendar year do not affect vacation earned; more than 90 days but no more than 180 days reduce vacation and vacation pay by one-fourth (¼); more than 180 days but no more than 270 days reduce by one-half (½); and more than 270 days disqualify the employee for vacation for that year only. For vacation timing and administration, vacation is treated as earned based on service; if ownership changes, the prior employer pays vacation earned up to the change date. Other contract provisions address leaves generally: after one (1) year, any leave of absence must be approved in writing except as otherwise provided, and failure to return at the end results in voluntary quit; service for wage progression is retained before the leave start but does not accrue during such leave beyond 30 days, resuming upon return. Sick/pregnancy/injury leaves for full-time employees employed at least 31 days may be granted up to 90 days with medical support, with extensions up to a cumulative 1 year in 90-day increments (or prorated for employees with less than one year service). Part-time-to-full-time conversion eligibility: effective November 16, 1980, all service from date of hire is counted for calculating vacation eligibility when a part-time employee becomes full-time after that date.

The Employer must contribute $191.11 per month to the Health and Welfare Trust Fund for each eligible employee who averages 24 hours per week over four consecutive calendar weeks (96 hours), and continue the same $191.11 monthly contribution for employees maintaining that weekly average; time off work while receiving the Employer’s sickness and/or accident benefits is counted as time worked for determining the 96 hours immediately before the first day of the month. Employer contributions begin on the 1st of the month following six full months of employment, but for employees covered by the District Trust Fund at hire, contributions start on the 1st of the month following the hire date. Effective November 1, 1984 and November 1, 1985, Health and Welfare contributions are increased only as necessary to maintain benefits in effect as of October 22, 1983, with no increase in benefits for the term of the Agreement. Upon termination, the Employer pays Trust Fund contributions for eligible employees for one month after termination (no coverage if discharged for cause), and for three full months after termination for employees receiving severance pay unless they obtain employment with another contributing employer. An actuarial study will be performed to determine the cost of continued contributions, and the Employer may elect to provide the required coverage directly. If required contributions are not made, the Trustees may require an additional 10% penalty.

Employer will continue participation and make contributions to the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union Industry Pension Trust Fund, which will maintain Treasury Department approval, with no obligation to contribute amounts that are not deductible for income tax purposes. Employer will also contribute $121.30 per calendar month per eligible employee to the jointly administered National Pension Trust Fund. “Eligible employee” means an employee averaging 24 hours per week over four consecutive calendar weeks (96 hours); eligibility begins on the first day of the first calendar month immediately following completion of those four weeks (the “eligibility date”). If contributions are discontinued under Section D, they are resumed on the first of the month following return from layoff or leave of absence. After termination, Employer will pay pension contributions for eligible employees for one month following termination. When Employer commences payments into the Pension Fund, affected employees under the Contract automatically cease participation in the Employer’s existing retirement plan; the Union also agrees that employees not already participants will withdraw and release any rights in the existing plan effective with the date Employer starts payments into the Fund. Separately, Employer will deduct from employee wages amounts designated by employees and forward them to a single individual retirement account to be established, at no cost to the Employer other than normal payroll deduction costs.

Security-related provisions primarily address work jurisdiction/assignment and enforcement: meat-handling at any central location operated by the Employer (in the counties listed in Paragraph A) that was previously done at the Employer’s retail markets must be performed by bargaining-unit members under this Contract’s wages, hours and conditions, unless the work falls under an existing collective bargaining agreement; new central-location work classifications may be created only after Employer–Union conferral on the wage rate, with the Employer able to set the classification/rate if no agreement is reached. Employees must perform seafood work only in the Seafood Department, and store scheduling/availability rights are recognized for the senior Seafood Clerk (first forty (40) hours). Disciplinary enforcement is included where work/time is not properly recorded: employees who perform unrecorded work or record another employee’s time are subject to discipline up to and including discharge. Additionally, upon assignment of bargaining-unit employees into management-exempt positions and later reassignment to the bargaining unit within six (6) months, the employee retains seniority. Seniority protections and transfers tied to job assignments (including Weighers/Wrappers transfer to Apprentice and Wrapper/Journeyman assignment/retention and recall rights) further govern who may be assigned these roles, and these assignment rules control access to protected schedules and work opportunities rather than limiting the Employer’s operational ability to handle meat/food at central points.

Training for apprentices requires that any Apprentice be at least eighteen (18) years of age and be trained to perform the duties of a Journeyman Meat Cutter, with the Employer assigning the Apprentice to various jobs to support qualification. The apprenticeship training period is two (2) years; if the Apprentice has not qualified as a Journeyman at the end of that period (as judged by the Employer), the apprenticeship may be extended for an additional six (6) months, during which the Apprentice is paid at the “Top Apprentice” rate. The Employer may advance an Apprentice to Journeyman status before the end of the training period if, in the Employer’s judgment, the Apprentice is qualified. Additionally, a Wrapper with one (1) year of full-time service with the Employer receives six (6) months of credit upon entrance to apprentice training.

The contract sets dispute/grievance procedures requiring prompt written handling: layoffs, discharges, recalls, and permanent transfers of full-time employees must be promptly reported by the Employer to the Union; grievances must be reduced to writing after completion of Step 2 to proceed to Step 3 and arbitration. The parties allow “general” issues affecting more than one employee to be initiated at any appropriate step rather than through the entire procedure, and require employees to use all contract rights and procedures in resolving complaints. Settlement authority rests with the Union Grievance Committee, and no arbitration may be pursued without its approval. For unresolved complaints, each side appoints one representative; if they cannot settle, either party may request within two (2) days a panel of seven (7) arbitrators from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service, and through a strike process a single arbitrator is selected; the arbitrator’s decision is binding and costs are split equally. For discharges for just cause, the Union may file a written complaint within five (5) working days; the matter must be promptly taken up, and if no agreement is reached within forty-eight (48) hours, it is referred to arbitration within twenty-four (24) hours. Arbitrators are prohibited from altering, amending, or changing any contract term.

The Safety-related provisions include: the parties agree there will be no discrimination against employees due to union membership or other protected characteristics (including age, race, creed, color, sex, or national origin), and that qualified employees age eighteen (18) or older have equal opportunity to work in covered job classifications. The Employer will furnish and maintain workplace safety supports and related necessities, including all necessary tools of the trade, and laundry and/or uniforms when required (with an exception allowing dacron or similar uniforms for female employees), and employees must replace uniforms in the event of loss and launder them themselves. The Employer must furnish and maintain a first aid kit in a designated place and check it monthly to replenish supplies. The Employer must provide safety guards on grinders and cube machines, and employees may not operate these machines without the guards in place; employees who do not comply may be disciplined up to discharge, without recourse to arbitration. Finally, employees cannot be required to take a polygraph test.

Miscellany provisions include: (1) an annual “Active Ballot Club” deduction made in January for employees who annually authorize it in writing, with remittance to the Local Union; (2) the Company’s agreement not to discourage union membership or lawful union activity and to inform new employees that operations are under a union contract; (3) mutual no-strike/no-lockout language—Union will not cause or sanction strikes, slowdowns, or stoppages, and the Employer will not lock out employees during the contract term; (4) employees are not required to cross a UFCW Local No. 408–sanctioned lawful labor picket line in a primary dispute, provided UFCW Local No. 408 gives the Employer at least 48 hours’ notice after primary picketing begins of its intent to sanction such picket line; (5) Union business agent access to working areas at reasonable times to interview covered employees while on duty; (6) Employer commitment not to conflict with contract terms via individual or collective agreements with covered employees; (7) provision of a bulletin board space selected by the Employer for Union notices; (8) if suit is needed to collect contributions, the Employer pays necessary court costs, reasonable attorneys’ fees, and a 10% penalty; and (9) a “me-too” clause allowing the Employer to adopt more advantageous terms and conditions if the Union later contracts with a major employer (Safeway or Lucky Stores d/b/a Eagle) in Harris County on terms more favorable than those in this Agreement.
